entities.name: Vienna State Opera house
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Vienna State Opera (Wiener Staatsoper) is the world's leading opera house, founded in 1869 on the Ringstrasse as the Imperial Court Opera, where Brahms, Bruckner, Mahler, Richard Strauss, and hundreds of other composers and conductors have shaped the history of classical music. The Staatsoper's position in Vienna's musical culture — the city that produced Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, Brahms, Bruckner, Mahler, and the Second Viennese School — makes it the institution most embedded in Western music's greatest tradition.

The building was designed by August Sicard von Sicardsburg and Eduard van der Nüll in Neo-Renaissance style, opening on 25 May 1869 with Mozart's Don Giovanni. The architects were so devastated by public criticism of the building's design that van der Nüll hanged himself (1868) and Sicardsburg died of grief two months later. The bombing by Allied forces in March 1945 destroyed the auditorium; reconstruction was completed in 1955, and the reopening with Beethoven's Fidelio on 5 November 1955 was broadcast live on Austrian radio as a national celebration of reconstruction.

Gustav Mahler's directorship (1897-1907) transformed the Staatsoper into the world's leading opera house through his insistence on theatrical integrity: Mahler covered the house lights, refused late arrivals, and conducted from memory. Herbert von Karajan's era (1957-1964) combined musical genius with autocratic management. The Staatsoper presents 50-60 different operas in a single season — a repertory system unmatched anywhere — with approximately 300 performances per year.
